title: Lake Land Employment Group of Akron, LLC v. Columber
lead: An existing at-will employee signed a noncompete without a raise, and Ohio’s divided high court held that continued employment supplied consideration while leaving the restriction’s reasonableness for remand.

actors.name: Lake Land Employment Group of Akron, LLC
actors.role: Employer suing to enforce a later-signed noncompete

actors.name: Lee Columber
actors.role: At-will employee who later opened a competing business

proceedings: Trial court granted employee summary judgment for no consideration; appellate court affirmed and certified conflict; Ohio Supreme Court reversed 4–3 and remanded for reasonableness and further proceedings.
limits: The 2004 judgment resolved consideration, not enforceability in every respect, breach, injunction, or damages. Columber could not recall an express continued-employment ultimatum; the majority legally characterized the proposal without finding particular words spoken.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Columber signed a restriction years after starting work
sections.cue: Introduce the terms and what did not change at signing.
paragraphs: Lake Land Employment Group employed Lee Columber from 1988 until 2001 in an at-will relationship. In September 1991, he signed a covenant restricting competitive activity for three years after termination within fifty miles of Akron. He received no raise, added benefits, or other remuneration, and his employment status otherwise remained unchanged. He continued working about ten more years.

Columber remembered little about presentation. He vaguely recalled being told to read and sign, acknowledged reading, and consulted no lawyer or other adviser. He could not remember whether Lake Land expressly said that continued employment depended on signing.

After Lake Land discharged him in 2001, he formed a corporation in a similar business. Lake Land sued for damages and an injunction, alleging violation. Columber admitted employment and execution but argued lack of consideration and excessive, unduly burdensome restrictions.

sections.title: The lower courts stopped at consideration
sections.cue: Identify the certified question and the issue left unexamined.
paragraphs: The trial court granted Columber summary judgment because he received no increase in compensation or change of status when signing. Having found no consideration, it did not assess whether three years and fifty miles were reasonable. The court of appeals affirmed but certified conflict with other Ohio appellate decisions.

The Ohio Supreme Court addressed whether continued employment alone could support a noncompete signed after at-will employment began. Chief Justice Moyer’s majority answered yes under the exchange it described, while preserving separate scrutiny of the restraint and other defenses.

sections.title: The majority treated future employment as a new exchange
sections.cue: Explain the actual forbearance theory rather than inventing a fixed-term promise.
paragraphs: Each party could lawfully end an at-will relationship. An employee could not insist on yesterday’s terms for all future work. An employer could propose lower compensation, leaving acceptance or departure to the employee; an employee could seek higher pay, leaving negotiation or termination to the employer. Earned wages remained governed by the prior agreement for work already done.

Presenting a noncompete similarly proposed new terms for continued employment. Employee assent and actual continuation exchanged the restriction for the employer’s forbearance from immediate termination. No separate raise was indispensable because the employee lacked an existing right to a fixed future period. That legal characterization did not depend on finding that Lake Land had uttered a particular ultimatum Columber could not recall.

The premise was an actual lawful termination right. An employer already bound for a fixed term, or one proposing unlawful termination, would raise different questions. The majority also rejected an undefined substantial-service-period test as uncertain at signing. Columber’s additional decade supported application here, but the rule imposed no specific numerical minimum.

sections.title: Consideration did not decide whether the restraint was reasonable
sections.cue: State the separate limits that justified remand.
paragraphs: The court declined to use consideration as a broad judicial comparison of bargaining values; adequacy ordinarily belonged to the parties. It nevertheless recognized the dual effects of noncompetes: protecting confidential information and productive cooperation, while potentially burdening livelihood and competition.

Those concerns remained within Ohio’s reasonableness framework. A restraint needed to protect legitimate interests without exceeding necessity, imposing undue employee hardship, or injuring the public. Courts could address excessive restrictions, and other invalidity grounds remained available. Because the trial court never reached duration and territory, an appellate finding of consideration did not establish those provisions’ validity or Columber’s breach.

sections.title: Resnick saw no new obligation; Pfeifer saw an unresolved duration problem
paragraphs: Justice Resnick would affirm. Lake Land retained the same power to discharge Columber immediately after signing, and he gained no new entitlement to work. Calling the unchanged relationship forbearance or renegotiation did not create an exchange in her view. She imagined an employee already possessing all useful training who was fired the next day: enforcing the restriction would reveal continued employment as an empty promise. Her objection concerned the existence of consideration, not just the small value of an acknowledged benefit.

Justice Pfeifer likewise rejected a termination threat as consideration and regarded the situation as coercive. He added a different difficulty: if the employer actually promised continued work in return for the covenant, that promise should alter at-will status for some period. Courts would then have to identify a reasonable duration of forbearance absent an agreed term. Separate payment could allow the covenant to stand independently from at-will employment. Neither proposed rule commanded the court.

sections.title: The employer won a chance to pursue enforcement, not a final remedy
sections.cue: Give the vote and limited result.
paragraphs: Moyer was joined by Lundberg Stratton, O’Connor, and Judge Handwork sitting for O’Donnell. Resnick, Francis E. Sweeney Sr., and Pfeifer dissented; Sweeney supplied no separate reported writing. By four to three, the court reversed and remanded for examination of reasonableness and further proceedings.

Lake Land prevailed on consideration and could continue the case. The Supreme Court neither enjoined Columber nor awarded damages nor approved the three-year, fifty-mile restraint. Its holding concerned this at-will exchange under Ohio law in 2004.
